title: Four kinds of devotees (7.13–7.19)
hook: people come to God in trouble, in curiosity, in need, and in knowing; the Gita calls all four noble

segments.voice: Yesterday, vijnana: one in a thousand, and the world strung like pearls on a thread. Today, who comes looking, and why.

Walk into a temple on any evening and look at the faces. A mother whose son is in the hospital. A student the night before an exam. A man whose shop isn't doing well, asking for a better year. A teenager who's just curious what all this is. An old woman who's been coming every day for sixty years and doesn't seem to need anything at all. Some people might say only one of them is here for the right reason. The Gita, chapter seven, looks at the same crowd, and says something more generous.
screen: `A MOTHER. A STUDENT. A SHOPKEEPER.` → `A CURIOUS TEENAGER.` → `SIXTY YEARS OF EVENINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the problem. The world is bewildered by the three gunas, Krishna says, the three strands of nature, and so it doesn't see him beyond them. His power of illusion is hard to cross, but those who turn to him cross it. Then verse sixteen. Four kinds of good people turn to me, Arjuna. The arta: the one in distress. The jijnasu: the one who wants to know. The artharthi: the one who seeks something, wealth, security, a good outcome. And the jnani: the one who knows. The mother, the teenager, the shopkeeper, the old woman. Here's what's striking. All four are called good people, and verse eighteen calls all of them noble: udara, generous, large-hearted. Nobody gets turned away for coming in trouble or coming with a request. But one stands out. The one who knows, verse seventeen says, always united, devoted to one alone, is the best. I am very dear to that one, and that one is dear to me. Verse eighteen goes further: the one who knows is my very self. And verse nineteen describes the journey there. At the end of many births, the one who knows takes refuge in me, seeing that Vasudeva is everything. Such a great soul, Krishna says, is very hard to find. So the ladder isn't a test you pass or fail. You can come in scared, or curious, or asking for a job. The door is open. And the Gita keeps walking you toward the fourth.
screen: `THE ONE IN DISTRESS.` · `THE ONE WHO WANTS TO KNOW.` · `THE ONE WHO SEEKS SOMETHING.` · `THE ONE WHO KNOWS.` · then, large: `ALL FOUR ARE NOBLE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself honestly which of the four you are today: here in some kind of trouble, out of curiosity, wanting something to change, or just to be here? There's no wrong answer; the Gita calls all four noble. Breathe with whatever you found, then, for the last part of the sit, let the reason go and simply sit, as the one who doesn't need anything.
Jnani. The one who knows, the fourth and dearest of four kinds of devotees: the one in distress, the one who wants to know, the one who seeks something, and the one who knows. All four noble.
Your line: the one who knows. Whatever brought you to the door, it's open. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindu temples welcome people who come for every reason: prayers in illness or trouble, questions, requests for success or a good year, and daily worship with no request at all; Gita 7.16 is often cited to honor all of them.

fork.reveal: all four: udarah, noble. then Krishna says the one who knows is dearest, his very self.

original.note: Sanskrit: jnani, the one who knows; the fourth and dearest of the four kinds of devotees (7.16–18).

trapdoor: what you thought: real devotion doesn't ask for anything.
what it means: people come in trouble, curiosity, need or knowing, and all four are noble; the one who knows is dearest.

what a scholar hears: 7.16 names arta, jijnasu, artharthi and jnani; 7.19's 'vasudevah sarvam iti', Vasudeva is all, is read by nondualist commentators as oneness and by devotional ones as total dependence on the Lord.
recall: a peace that doesn't come and go
the one who dwells in the body

chat.says: Is it wrong to go to temple only when you need something?
options: No: the Gita calls all four kinds of seekers noble, even those who ask.
Yes: the Gita says only the one who knows is truly welcome there.
No: the Gita says asking for things is the very best reason to go.
chat.meaning: Gita 7.16–18: the one in distress, the curious, the one who asks and the one who knows are all called noble. The one who knows is dearest.

arta.meaning: the one who comes in distress

jijnasu.meaning: the one who wants to know

artharthi.meaning: the one who seeks something, like security or a good outcome

jnani.meaning: the one who knows; the dearest of the four
